result.summary: Capaneus lies dead after Jove's thunderbolt, and the Furies Tisiphone and Megaera drive Polynices and Eteocles to fight each other. The brothers kill one another despite pleas from Adrastus, Jocasta, Antigone and Piety. Jocasta kills herself, Creon seizes the throne, bans burial of the Argives and exiles Oedipus to Cithaeron.

scenes.title: Capaneus falls; Argives routed
scenes.summary: After Capaneus is struck down, Thebes revives and the Achaeans flee, harried by the Thebans.
scenes.stakes: The Argive army faces slaughter in flight.

scenes.title: Tisiphone summons Megaera
scenes.summary: Tisiphone calls her sister up from the underworld and they divide the brothers between them; Jove turns his gaze from the coming crime.
scenes.stakes: The brothers' kinship and the world's moral order are threatened.

scenes.title: Polynices resolves to duel
scenes.summary: Haunted by Argia's phantom, Polynices tells Adrastus he will fight his brother, and the Fury sends him off on a horse.
scenes.stakes: Polynices risks his life and the chance that his body goes unburied.

scenes.title: Eteocles, Creon and Jocasta
scenes.summary: Eteocles' sacrifice is marred by omens, and Creon, grieving Menoeceus, taunts him to fight. Jocasta rushes to stop him.
scenes.stakes: Eteocles risks his throne and his life, and Creon's grief is turned on him.

scenes.title: Pleas fail; brothers meet
scenes.summary: Jocasta and Antigone plead, and Polynices wavers, but Eteocles bursts out and the two charge each other.
scenes.stakes: The brothers risk killing each other.

scenes.title: Adrastus flees; Piety driven off
scenes.summary: Adrastus fails to part them and flees. Piety briefly halts the armies until Tisiphone drives her away.

scenes.title: The brothers kill each other
scenes.summary: The brothers fight, and each mortally wounds the other, Eteocles by a last deceit. They die together.

scenes.title: Oedipus mourns; Jocasta dies
scenes.summary: Blind Oedipus finds his dead sons and wants to die, but Antigone has hidden the swords. Jocasta stabs herself.
scenes.stakes: Oedipus's will to live; Jocasta's life.

scenes.title: Creon's rule; Oedipus exiled
scenes.summary: Creon takes the throne, forbids burial for the Argives and banishes Oedipus to Cithaeron despite Antigone's plea. The Argives slip away by night.
scenes.stakes: Oedipus faces exile; the Argive dead lie unburied.

alias_notes.explanation: Title of Jove as wielder of the thunderbolt.
Epithet of the war god Mars, addressed in sentence 10.
Epithet of Bacchus, god of wine.
Patronymic of Hercules, grandson of Alcaeus.

notable_quotes.reason: The poet prays that posterity forget the horror of the brothers' fratricide.
Oedipus's breakdown as nature and grief finally overcome him.

analysis.text: Fraternal hatred, driven by Furies yet chosen by the brothers, overturns piety and family. Even gods look away from the crime.
Statius writes in the Flavian period, when civil war and kin-slaying were fresh Roman memories, so the Theban duel echoes Rome's own civil strife.

legacy.text: The mutual death of Eteocles and Polynices became a standard image of fratricidal war, later echoed by Dante in his image of their divided funeral flame in the Inferno.

fun_facts.text: The Thebaid was a favourite of medieval readers, and Dante made Statius his guide in Purgatorio.

language_notes.text: Levin-fire means lightning; the thunderbolt that killed Capaneus is meant.
Phlegra was the battlefield where the gods fought the Giants; Jove is likened to a weary victor, with Enceladus a Giant buried under Aetna.
The defiler of Apollo's mother is Tityos, who assaulted Latona; in the underworld vultures feed on his ever-regrowing liver.
Massylian refers to the Massyli, a North African people, a region known for lions. Agenor's warriors are the Thebans, descended from Agenor, Cadmus's father.
Eurymedon, son of Pan, uses panic terrors, the sudden irrational fear associated with Pan. Alatreus is a young Theban fighter beside his father.
Gradivus is a title of Mars, god of war.
Pelasgians here means the Argives, using an old name for Greeks.
Hercules (son of Amphitryon's wife) is the model for the Tirynthian soldiers, who wear lion skins and carry clubs like his Nemean gear.
Enyeus is the name of a trumpeter on the Argive tower; the name echoes Enyo, a war goddess.
"Stygian blade" means a sword belonging to the Styx, the underworld river; "caerulean" means dark blue. The serpent is the leader among the snakes of her hair.
"The Father glanced again at his Aetnaean fires": Jove, startled by the omen, looks again at the thunderbolts forged beneath Etna.
"Belauded" means heavily praised; the dead of Dis's realm honour Capaneus, who defied Jove and was struck down by his lightning.
Lethe is the underworld river of forgetfulness; the "swarms" are the newly slain ghosts crowding its bank.
Enyo is a Greek war goddess, here a companion of Mars; Tisiphone says war's glory can go to them, not her.
"Levin" is an old word for lightning; she means Capaneus's defiance of Jove's thunderbolt.
"His mother's words" refers to Jocasta, mother of the brothers, and Antigone, their sister, who both plead for peace.
"He" is Oedipus, who blinded himself and cursed his sons; the Furies were called on to avenge his eyes. He now softens as a father.
Jove lists earlier crimes: Tantalus serving his son to the gods, Lycaon's impious sacrifice, and Mycenae's feud of Atreus and Thyestes, which made the sun turn back.
The torch Argia carries is a funeral torch, in grim contrast to the marriage torches expected at a wedding; the poet's aside calls it an omen.
Acheron is a river of the underworld; "Fury of yawning Acheron" marks her as an infernal spirit of vengeance.
"Corslet" is body armour covering the chest.
The speech breaks off mid-sentence as Polynices cannot finish his complaint; he turns abruptly to challenge his brother.
His sightless father is Oedipus, who blinded himself; the mother and sisters are Jocasta, Antigone and Ismene.
Tydeus, Polynices' ally, died at Thebes; Tegea and Parrhasian caves are in Arcadia, home of Atalanta, mother of Parthenopaeus, another dead ally.
Hippomedon fought at the river Ismenos near Thebes; Capaneus was struck down by Jove's thunderbolt while scaling the walls.
Bistonian snows and the mountains Haemus and Rhodope are in Thrace, known for harsh winters.
"Inachian" means Argive, from Inachus, the legendary river-god and first king of Argos.
The Evil Spirit is the family's curse, the Fury that has driven the house of Oedipus to mutual hatred since his curses on his sons.
The spouse is Oedipus, who blinded himself on learning his crimes. Jocasta says his blindness spares him this sight, while her own eyes must suffer it.
She will stand in the gateway as an ill omen, meaning he must pass over her body to attack the city that holds her.
Her womb is the one that bore him; trampling it recalls the earlier incest and shows how monstrous the attack would be.
Stygian gods are the gods of the underworld, named for the river Styx. Oedipus had called on the Furies to curse his sons.
Ogygian is a poetic epithet for Thebes, from the legendary early king Ogyges.
The yearly pact was the agreement that the brothers would rule Thebes in alternate years. Eteocles broke it by refusing to yield the throne.
Argive home refers to Argos, where Polynices married Argia. Tyrian means Theban, since Thebes was founded by Cadmus, who came from Tyre.
Maeonian means Lydian, from a region of Asia Minor famous for fine dyed and woven textiles.
Martian means belonging to Mars, the god of war.
Ogygian means Theban; Ogyges was a legendary early king of Boeotia, so the ghosts are Thebes' own dead.
Sons of Inachus and Tyre: Argive descent (Inachus, river-god and first king of Argos) for Polynices, Phoenician Tyre through Cadmus for Eteocles.
The Cyanean rocks are the Symplegades, clashing rocks at the Black Sea entrance that the Argo passed; Pontus is the sea.
The third heir of the world is Pluto (Dis), who drew the underworld in the lot-casting among Jove's brothers; Adrastus' fear is likened to his.
Promethean skill refers to Prometheus, who in legend moulded mankind from clay.
Pyrrha and Deucalion repopulated the earth after the flood by throwing stones that became people.
Bacchus made war on Thebes when King Pentheus rejected his worship, and the maddened women tore Pentheus apart.
Tisiphone lists Thebes' earlier crimes: Cadmus' dragon-slaying and sowing of teeth, the Sphinx, Oedipus' killing of his father Laius, and his marriage to Jocasta.
Oedipus, blinded by his own hand, cursed his sons for dishonouring him; the gods are said to have heard that curse, which drives the brothers' strife.
"The cloudy South wind" is the storm-bringing Auster; the ships are locked by the gale, not by choice.
"Corslet" is a piece of body armour; its lowest rim, fringed with feathered (scale-like) plates, leaves the groin poorly guarded.
Cithaeron is the mountain near Thebes, tied to its myths; its being "startled" means the shout echoes across the Theban landscape.
The Gnosian judge of the Agenorean line is Minos of Crete (Gnosos), son of Europa, daughter of Agenor; he judges the dead in the underworld.
Tartarus and Erebus are names for the underworld's regions of punishment and darkness.
"Living corpse" is a paradox: Oedipus is alive but looks like the dead, blinded and filthy with old blood.
Avernus is a lake near Naples and a name for the underworld; its "furrower" is the ferryman Charon, who rows the dead across.
"Late after so long time" means after so long a delay; Oedipus says natural affection has come to him very late.
The prayers and curses refer to Oedipus's curse that his sons would divide their inheritance by the sword; the Fates carried it out.
Dis is the king of the underworld (Pluto). Laius is Oedipus's father, whom he killed unknowingly.
"Her dire couch" refers to her marriage bed with her own son Oedipus, the source of her shame.
Erigone hanged herself from grief after her father Icarius was killed; the story is told as a parallel to Ismene's sorrow.
Amphion was legendary builder of Thebes' walls; Cadmus its founder. Both names stand for the Theban kingship.
Thebans of the old royal line sprang from the dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus, and were sacred to Mars; Menoeceus, Creon's son, had sacrificed himself for Thebes.
Aonia is a poetic name for Boeotia, the region around Thebes; hence 'Aonians' means Thebans.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks, here the Argive army lying unburied.
'Avaunt' is an archaic command meaning 'be gone!'; 'Ogygian' means Theban, from the legendary king Ogyges.
Oedipus, who killed his father and married his mother, is called a 'hateful omen' and bearer of Furies, avenging spirits that pursued his family.
Bitterly ironic curse: Oedipus wishes on Creon his own fate, marrying and begetting sons, and clinging to life when trapped.
Cithaeron is the mountain where the infant Oedipus was left to die, so exile there returns him to his beginnings.
Pelasgians is a poetic term for the Greeks, here the defeated Argives.

context_notes.text: Capaneus was struck by Jove's thunderbolt while scaling Thebes' wall and defying the gods.
Thebans had been praying in temples, holding children, during the siege; Capaneus' death ends their terror.
Tiryns was a city in the Argolid, so these soldiers are Argives imitating Hercules, who was born in Thebes.
Tisiphone is one of the three Furies, avenging spirits from the underworld; Megaera is another. Here they drive Eteocles and Polynices to fight each other.
Dis is the king of the underworld, here called the Furies' "Stygian father."
Cocytus is a river of the underworld, the "river of wailing."
Rhipaean mountains were imagined in the far north, so the North wind comes from there; Libya stands for the hot south.
The Ledaean brethren are Castor and Pollux, sons of Leda, who became the constellation Gemini.
Argia is Polynices' wife and Adrastus' daughter; he married her while in exile at Argos, which led to the Argive war on Thebes.
Adrastus is king of Argos and Polynices' father-in-law, who led the expedition to restore Polynices to the Theban throne.
Denial of burial rites, or leaving a body to birds, was a dreadful fate in antiquity, so he asks for his ashes to be recovered.
Adrastus is the king of Argos who sheltered Polynices and led the Argive army against Thebes on his behalf.
Antigone is the sister of the brothers. Actor is her aged attendant.
Argia is Polynices' wife and Adrastus' daughter. Her woven cloak links him to his Argive allies.
Bellona is the Roman goddess of war. The Maid is Minerva, shown with the Gorgon's head on her aegis.
Adrastus, king of Argos, is father-in-law to both Polynices and Tydeus, and has led the Argive army against Thebes.
Piety (Pietas) is a personified goddess of dutiful love toward family, gods and country.
Tisiphone is a Fury, an avenging spirit of the underworld who has driven the brothers' hatred throughout the poem.
The speaker is Polynices, the exiled brother, who has marched on Thebes to claim the throne Eteocles refused to share as agreed.
The Furies were avenging spirits who punished crimes, especially against kin; they have driven this feud, yet here need do nothing more.
The Stygian goddesses are the Furies, tied to the river Styx of the underworld; the poet prays they spare mankind further such horrors.
The maid is Antigone, Oedipus's daughter, who guides him after his self-blinding.
Jocasta is Oedipus's wife and mother; the sword once belonged to her first husband Laius.
After Eteocles and Polynices kill each other, their uncle Creon inherits the throne of Thebes.
Denying burial was a grave impiety, since unburied dead could not find rest in the underworld.
Antigone, Oedipus' daughter, serves as his guide and pleads for him with Creon.

literary_notes.text: Capaneus' huge fallen body is compared to the giant Tityos in the underworld, stressing his size and punishment.
The Argives hear thunder in their helmets and see Jove himself pursuing them, showing their terror.
Thebans are likened to bears and wolves scavenging a lion's kill, implying they profit from Jove's work, not their own strength.
The narrator suddenly addresses Mars, marking the reversal of fortune with exclamation.
Returning clouds, winds and the surge over sand illustrate the tide-like shifts of battle.
The trumpeter who once urged attack now signals retreat, and the trumpet sounds on after his death.
Nature answers her rising: as the underworld's darkness thins, daylight above dims, as if the two realms swap light and shadow.
Tisiphone's admission of weariness shows that even a Fury can be worn down, which makes Megaera's fresh rage necessary.
The sisters parting are likened to the South and North winds clashing, which conveys their destructive force and the ruin they cause.
Jove abruptly commands the gods not to look, a dramatic address that shows how unspeakable the coming crime is.
The loss of the clear light as Jove looks away stands for the moral darkness that falls on the world.
The phantom with a mournful torch hints at Polynices' coming death and funeral, and at Argia's later grief.
The Fury physically lashes him, externalizing his madness and doom as a divine agent driving him toward fratricide.
Tears of the listeners are compared to melting Thracian snows swelling rivers, conveying abundant, flowing grief.
The Fury sets him on the horse to hasten his death; his pale glance back shows he senses her presence, despite his claimed resolve.
Jocasta opens with a cry of horror, and a run of questions follows that shows her desperation.
Her warning that he will prevail but must first trample her anticipates the brothers' bloody end.
The Fury and the Fiend act as characters who resist Antigone's plea and burst the gate, so the family curse takes bodily form.
Polynices' envy of his brother's gear and his own fine cloak show the pride and rivalry behind the quarrel.
Even the war gods flee, a sweeping image that makes this fratricide too terrible for war itself.
The god of the dead summons ghosts to watch, making the underworld an audience that delights in the living's cruelty.
Adrastus' pleas are compared to the sea failing to stop the clashing rocks, stressing how futile persuasion is.
Piety appears as a grieving goddess in disordered dress, mourning like a sister or mother, which dramatizes the loss of familial feeling.
Piety's exclamations cry out against humanity and Prometheus' creation, conveying despair.
Tisiphone's hissing hydras and torch show her menace, while Piety shrinking and veiling her face shows how powerless she is.
Two ships locked by storm and sinking together compare the brothers' entangled, mutually destructive fight, foreshadowing their joint death.
Raging boars watched by a hunter portray the brothers as beasts, with the anxious hunter standing for helpless onlookers.
The Furies, normally agents of vengeance, are reduced to admiring spectators because human hatred outdoes their own.
Eteocles feigns death to deceive his brother, using a last fraud as his weapon.
Polynices believes he has won and moves to claim spoils, while the reader sees the hidden, dying Eteocles raise his weapon.
The poet turns to the Furies and begs that this crime be forgotten, voicing his own horror in the narrator's voice.
Oedipus emerging into daylight is compared to Charon leaving the underworld, frightening sun and stars, stressing his deathlike, unnatural presence.
Oedipus addresses Nature directly as if she were a person who has defeated him.
Oedipus blames madness, Furies and family for his ills and denies his own responsibility, though he spoke the curse himself.
The comparison to Erigone sets Ismene's grief within a mythic pattern of daughters mourning fathers.
The narrator's exclamation laments the war's pointless outcome: the brothers died only to raise Creon.
Calling the throne one that 'brings death to tyrants' hints at Creon's own downfall.
The narrator addresses Fortune directly, sarcastically asking what her kindness achieves now.
Old age 'falling from him' conveys rage restoring Oedipus' strength, if only for a moment.
Oedipus taunts Creon to kill him, scorning exile as weak cruelty and showing he fears no punishment.
The aged lion compares Oedipus' fading strength and surviving menace, roused by a sound as by Creon's insults.
